news.title: [SMM Analysis] Those asking "how far will sulfur fall" should consider at least four questionsAfter sulfur prices dropped sharply from their earlier highs, the market kept circling back to the same question: where will the price settle? It seems simple, but it is the wrong question to ask first. Sulfur's price is never set by a single answer, but by at least four independent questions. Before asking "how far will it fall," these four questions have to be thought through. 1. First, sort out: is this one question, or several? Treating "how far will sulfur fall" as a single question is where most current judgments begin — and it is the biggest mistake. Sulfur's price is never set by a single force. The import channel, domestic supply, downstream substitution, and the shift in demand structure each pull in their own direction, on their own timeline. So the forces that determine the price are not one point, but several independent questions. This is why market views diverge so sharply: some see support abroad, some see pressure at home, some point to low inventories, some to shrinking demand. They are not arguing about the same thing — each is answering one question and then generalizing it into "the price of sulfur." ​ The disagreement stems from a category error, not from conflicting facts. 2. The first question: the import channel, locked by the home-abroad price gap Sulfur is heavily import-dependent, and whether the import channel stays open directly sets the marginal cost of domestic supply. Once the home-abroad price gap inverts far enough, importing becomes unprofitable and voluntary imports stall. At that point the domestic market is no longer priced by "international price plus freight," but by domestic supply "circulating internally." This shift hides a paradox that is often missed: until the overseas price returns to a level that reopens the import window, the domestic market leans on domestic supply — and much of that supply is locked up by the guaranteed-supply mechanism, leaving only a limited portion genuinely available in the open market. The inversion is therefore no longer just a price phenomenon of "support abroad, pressure at home"; it is actively cutting off the import channel and shrinking domestic tradable supply. This question does not depend on when global supply and demand rebalance, but on when the truly tradable supply outside the guaranteed-supply system is exhausted. It asks about supply elasticity, not demand recovery. 3. The second question: the layer of demand that is permanently shaved off A common assumption is that once prices fall far enough, downstream margins recover and demand returns. This assumption misses a structural change — substitution is shaving off a portion of demand permanently, not cyclically. Sulfur's largest downstream is phosphate fertilizer, and the phosphate industry is migrating from "buying sulfur to make acid" toward "making acid from by-product resources." Once this substitution reaches scale, the demand it removes will not return simply because sulfur gets cheaper — because the driver is not only cost, but also environmental constraints and the strategic goal of resource self-sufficiency. This question is the opposite of the first in nature: the first is cyclical — prices recover, margins heal, demand returns; the second is structural — the demand curve shifts down as a whole, and what comes back is permanently less than before. Its implication for price is that even if sulfur rebounds in the future, the historical level it can return to is permanently lower. 4. The third question: the short-term level of the domestic spot market If the question is narrowed to "how much further can spot fall in the near term," the answer becomes clearer. After a rapid slide, the domestic spot market has shown signs of stabilizing. This stabilization comes from several forces stacking up: supply constraints from cost inversion, the relative tightness of tradable supply, and the approach of winter stocking. But the nature of this level must be understood clearly: it is stabilization brought by structural supply tightness and market sentiment, not a demand-driven reversal. The real demand downstream — phosphate operating rates, chemical purchasing — has not fundamentally improved. This short-term level is therefore fragile; its durability depends on whether expectations are realized, not on whether demand itself can support it. 5. The fourth question: the shift in demand structure, rewriting the premise of the first three There is one more variable that is easy to overlook. It belongs to none of the first three questions, yet it sets all three positions in motion: sulfur's demand structure is migrating. Sulfur's downstream is spreading from the traditional fertilizer sector into new energy and fine chemicals. This migration means sulfur's demand elasticity and pricing logic can no longer be explained by the fertilizer seasonality framework. When the demand structure shifts this way, judging sulfur's level by "the fertilizer cycle" may be wrong from the premise. The party that sets the price is changing, and so is its rhythm. A commodity being redefined is having its pricing logic redefined too. This is not a level that can be extrapolated from history — it is a force that erases the original scale on each of the preceding questions. 6. Putting the four questions together The answer then emerges: sulfur's price is not locked by a single answer, but by four questions stacked in layers. The import-channel question, set by the home-abroad gap and domestic guaranteed supply, locks in short-term supply elasticity. The substituted-demand question, set by the spread of substitution, locks in the medium- to long-term position of the demand curve. The short-term spot question, set by sentiment and structural supply, may already have an answer — but it is fragile. The demand-structure question, set by the direction of downstream migration, is rewriting the scale of every question before it. Near term, watch tradable supply and winter stocking; medium term, watch the pace of substitution and new capacity; long term, watch the direction of demand-structure migration. For different participants, the "question" that matters is different: traders care about the window between import contraction and spot tightness; downstream producers care about whether their substitution units come online before the wave of new capacity; long-term investors face a more fundamental question — when substitution permanently takes over a portion of demand, will sulfur's pricing logic be the same as it is today? The price will not give a single answer, because it was never a single question. The real question is not "where will the price settle," but "for me, which question is decisive." Figure that out, and the question is already half answered.Nov 11, 2026 17:47 (GMT+8)

news.title: Connected Minerals advances niobium drilling at Bailundo project[SMM Niobium Flash] Connected Minerals has advanced its maiden diamond drilling programme at the Bailundo Carbonatite Project in Angola, where it is exploring for niobium and rare earth elements. In its 29 October quarterly report, the Australian-listed company reported that approximately 937 metres had been drilled across 14 diamond drill collars as of 27 October. Samples from the first seven holes had been dispatched for laboratory analysis, with initial results expected in mid-November. The company also acquired historical exploration records containing 10 diamond drill holes totalling 3,414.4 metres. Historical results include an intersection of 205.5 metres grading 1.0% niobium pentoxide (Nb₂O₅) from surface. The current drilling programme is intended to test the continuity of the mineralisation and improve understanding of the deposit's geological characteristics ahead of further exploration. Connected Minerals holds an indirect 80% interest in the project and is targeting a maiden JORC mineral resource estimate by the end of 2027, subject to drilling results and technical validation. Importantly, the reported high-grade intersections are historical results and should not be confused with assays from the ongoing drilling programme. No new assay results were confirmed in the latest company report reviewed.7 hours ago
